item.research_question: How can high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and high-entropy oxides (HEOs) be synthesized and applied as protective layers for interconnectors and anode components in hydrocarbon-fueled solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) to overcome issues like chromium evaporation and carbon deposition?
item.material_system: FeCoNiMnCu high-entropy alloy coating converted to (FeCoNiMnCu)3O4 spinel; HEA/GDC anode catalyst containing Ni, Co, Cu, Fe, Mn on Gd-doped CeO2 (GDC) support
item.processing_route: Vacuum induction melting to create sputtering target; magnetron sputtering deposition of 4 μm coating on SUS 430 steel at 200 °C for 2 h (1.2 kW power, 0.13 Pa Ar); thermal conversion at 800 °C for 10 weeks (1680 h total); co-precipitation of HEA from nitrate precursors with citric acid, calcination at 500 °C for 6 h, mixing with GDC (65:35 wt ratio)
item.test_conditions: Oxidation in air at 800 °C for up to 10 weeks; SOFC cell testing at 750 °C; Steam reforming of methane (SRM) in fixed-bed tube reactor at 700–800 °C with GHSV of 45,000 1/h
key_findings: After 10 weeks of oxidation at 800 °C, the FeCoNiMnCu coating converted to a uniform (FeCoNiMnCu)3O4 spinel layer with a surface Cr concentration of only 4.34%.
The area-specific resistance (ASR) of the oxidized HEA coating decreased from 8.21 mΩ·cm² after 1 week to 6.59 mΩ·cm² after 10 weeks at 800 °C.
The ASR of the scale was 17 mΩ·cm² at 600 °C, which is well below the accepted limit of 0.1 Ω·cm².
The HEA/GDC catalyst showed excellent stability during SRM, whereas Ni/YSZ and Ni/GDC catalysts rapidly degraded with time.
After 30 h of SOFC cell testing, the post-test HEA/GDC anode layer was carbon-free, while the Ni/YSZ anode contained 17.3% carbon.
The reforming rate of the HEA/GDC catalyst increased from 27% at 700 °C to 42% at 800 °C.
A current density of approximately 100 mA/cm² was achieved at 750 °C in the SOFC cell test using the HEA/GDC anode.
item.mechanism: The high-entropy spinel coating thermally converted from the HEA effectively blocks chromium out-diffusion from the substrate, reducing the growth of the Cr-rich oxide layer and lowering electrical resistivity. The HEA-based anode demonstrates superior carbon resistance because the mingled sites of multiple transition metals prevent the deposition and fiber growth of carbon that typically damages Ni-based anodes.
item.limitations: The conductivity of the (FeCoNiMnCu)3O4 spinel was not measured directly in the study; the reforming rate of the HEA/GDC catalyst was lower than that of the Ni-based catalysts at 750 °C.
item.future_work: Further study and development of carbon-resistant anodes for hydrocarbon-fueled SOFCs with direct internal reforming is needed based on the promising results.
quotes: The coating of 4 μm in thickness was deposited on the SUS 430 steel substrate under sputtering power of 1.2 kW for 2 h at 200 °C in a chamber with an Ar pressure of 0.13 Pa.
The surface of the post-test HEA/GDC anode layer was carbon-free.
The high-entropy spinel coating thermally converted from the HEA coating showed it was capable of effectively blocking Cr out-diffusion.

item.research_question: How does high configurational entropy and multi-cation doping affect the ionic conductivity, activation energy, and structural stability of fluorite- and pyrochlore-structured high-entropy oxides (HEOs) compared to conventional SOFC electrolytes like YSZ and GDC?
item.material_system: Fluorite-structured HEOs: (Hf0.25Zr0.25Ce0.25Y0.25)O2-δ (HEFO1), (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ce0.2)(Y0.2Yb0.2)O2-δ (HEF04B), (Hf0.327Ce0.456Zr0.217)0.85Yb0.15O1.93 (Yb-15(1)); Pyrochlore-structured HEOs: (Nd0.2Sm0.2Gd0.2Dy0.2Y0.2)2Zr2O7 (HEC-1 to HEC-5); Ceria-based HEOs: CeGdDySmPrO2-δ, CeGdLaSmPrO2-δ
item.processing_route: High-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering and annealing in air at 1500 °C with furnace cooling (50 °C/min); Solid-state reaction method with final sintering at 1500–1700 °C; Sol-gel method followed by compaction and free sintering at 1500 °C in air
item.test_conditions: Electrical conductivity measured in dry air in the temperature range of 650–850 °C; Conductivity measured at 600 °C and 800 °C; Activation energy determined in temperature ranges of 300–750 °C and 170–560 °C
key_findings: Conductivity of fluorite HEOs (e.g., HEFO1) at 850 °C ranged from 1.9 to 2.9 mS/cm, significantly lower than the 30 mS/cm observed for YSZ.
Activation energies for HEO fluorites were 1.14–1.29 eV, higher than the 1.0 eV for YSZ.
The highest conductivity for ZrO2-based HEOs (CCFO2) was 5.35 × 10−4 S/cm at 600 °C with an activation energy of 0.66 eV.
Pyrochlore HEC-5 achieved a conductivity of 7.1 × 10−3 S/cm at 800 °C, higher than base low and medium zirconates.
Ceria-based HEOs (CeGdLaSmPrO2-δ) reached 0.001 S/cm at 510 °C with activation energies of 0.52–0.53 eV.
Increasing the cation radius ratio r(A3+)/r(B4+) in pyrochlore HEOs increased conductivity due to higher mobile vacancy concentration.
Raman spectroscopy showed a blue shift in the main band for HEOs, indicating lattice compression, and an increase in the 570 cm−1 band intensity indicating more oxygen vacancies.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that ionic conductivity in HEOs is inhibited by local crystal lattice distortion caused by relatively high ionic radius differences (δrion), which lowers oxygen mobility. Additionally, high deviation of oxygen non-stoichiometry from the optimal 4% value leads to defect association, reducing free charge carriers. In pyrochlore structures, higher conductivity is ensured by a continuous and energetically favorable pathway for oxygen jumps between 48f-sites, which cannot form in fluorite structures due to random cation/anion occupation.
item.limitations: The high cost and limited resources of scandium and gallium in alternative electrolytes; poor chemical stability of Bi2O3-based electrolytes in reducing atmospheres; reduction of Ce4+ to Ce3+ in doped ceria under anode conditions causing power efficiency loss; difficulty in stabilizing fluorite HEOs without deterioration of transport properties; low conductivity of HEOs compared to conventional electrolytes in many cases.
item.future_work: Further efforts should be applied to the search for new methods to stabilize fluorite HEOs without deterioration of their transport properties; HEOs with pyrochlore structure are highly stable and entropy disordering enhances transport properties, providing a point for future development; HEO proton and dual conductors with perovskite structure are highly demanded.
quotes: The authors argue that decreasing the conductivity may be related to a smaller gran size of HE ceramics as well as to a high doping level, exceeding the optimal value for the ZrO2-based ceramic equal to 8–10 mol.%
The authors concluded that ionic conductivity in HEOs can be inhibited due to lowering the oxygen mobility, caused by a local crystal lattice distortion due to relatively high δrion values
In pyrochlore structure, oxygen that jumps from 48f-site to 48f-site can form a continuous and energetically favorable pathway which can play a major role in the increase in ionic conductivity.
